title: Accessible Forms and Errors
summary: A visible red error message means nothing to a screen reader unless it's explicitly wired to its field. Learn the label strategies, aria-describedby error association, and live regions that make dynamic form feedback actually accessible.

slides.markdown:
Forms are where accessibility gaps have the most direct, concrete cost: a user who can't figure out why a form won't submit doesn't get to complete the task at all — this isn't a degraded experience, it's a hard stop. [Native validation](forms-and-validation) gets you a long way, but the native error UI (a browser tooltip, gone the moment the field loses focus) isn't sufficient for a production form's real error UX.

This topic covers the layer that makes form errors genuinely accessible: choosing the right labeling strategy, wiring errors to their fields so a screen reader actually announces them, and using live regions correctly so dynamic feedback is heard without unexpectedly yanking the user's focus somewhere they didn't ask to go.

The throughline: a form that *looks* like it has good error handling and a form that's actually accessible are two different bars, and the gap between them is almost always in the plumbing a sighted user never notices is missing.

slides.subTitle: <label for> vs aria-label vs aria-labelledby
slides.markdown:
| Approach | How it works | When to use it |
|---|---|---|
| `<label for="id">` | a real, visible `<label>` element linked to the input's id | the default — always prefer this when there's visible label text |
| `aria-label="..."` | a string provided directly as the accessible name, with no visible label text at all | icon-only controls with no text on screen (a search input with just a magnifying-glass icon) |
| `aria-labelledby="id"` | points to another element's id and uses *its* text content as the accessible name | when visible text already exists elsewhere in the markup and shouldn't be duplicated |

`<label for>` (or wrapping the input directly) has a real, often-overlooked usability bonus beyond accessibility: it expands the input's clickable/tappable target to include the label text itself, which matters enormously for small checkboxes and radio buttons on a touch screen. `aria-label` should be treated as a last resort specifically because it's invisible on screen — anyone relying on a translation tool, or simply glancing at the rendered page, has no way to know it exists, unlike a real label.

A red border and adjacent error text convey the error visually but nothing to a screen reader unless the two are explicitly linked: ```html Enter a valid email address ``` `aria-describedby` tells assistive tech "this id's text content is additional description for this field," so a screen reader announces the label, then the field type, then the error text, all together when the field receives focus — the user doesn't have to go hunting elsewhere on the page for why their input failed. `aria-invalid="true"` separately flags the field itself as currently failing validation, which many screen readers announce as "invalid" alongside the description. Both attributes are only correct while the error is real — they need to be added when validation fails and explicitly removed once the field becomes valid again, the same staleness discipline covered for other ARIA state attributes.

`aria-describedby` handles an error that exists *when the user reaches that field*. It doesn't help with feedback that appears *while the user is somewhere else* — a form-wide error banner that appears above the form after a failed submission, while focus is still sitting on the submit button.

`aria-live="polite"` on a region announces changes to its content automatically, without moving focus there — the screen reader finishes whatever it was currently saying, then announces the new content, then returns control to the user exactly where they were. This is the right choice for most form feedback: a "3 errors found" summary, a save confirmation, a character-count update.

`aria-live="assertive"` interrupts immediately rather than waiting — reserved for genuinely urgent cases (a session about to expire, a failed payment) since it's disruptive by design; using it for routine feedback is a common overcorrection that makes a form feel like it's constantly interrupting the user. Both variants only announce **changes** to the region's content after it's already present in the DOM on page load — injecting the entire live region into the DOM for the first time, error text and all, in the same instant doesn't reliably trigger an announcement in every screen reader, since there was no prior content for it to compare against.

slides.sectionTitle: A form submission with an error, from a screen reader's perspective
slides.markdown:
Trace what a screen reader user actually experiences on a failed submission, versus what a sighted user sees. A sighted user sees a red banner appear at the top and red text under the offending field, and their eyes are drawn there automatically. A screen reader user's focus is still sitting wherever they last were — often the submit button — and nothing draws their attention anywhere unless the implementation explicitly does so.

A correct implementation: an `aria-live="polite"` summary region (already present in the DOM, empty, before submission) gets populated with "1 error found: Email is required," which gets announced without moving focus; each invalid field simultaneously gets `aria-invalid="true"` and `aria-describedby` pointing at its own inline error. The user hears the summary immediately, and can then navigate directly to the problem field — often via a link inside the error summary itself that moves focus to the field on activation.

![Sighted vs screen-reader timelines for the same failed form submission](assets/form-error-two-timelines.svg)

assets.alt: Sighted vs screen-reader timelines for the same failed form submission

slides.markdown:
A field styled with only a red border to indicate an error fails for several real, distinct groups at once, not just one edge case: color-blind users (red/green is the single most common form of color blindness, and a red border can be indistinguishable from a neutral one), screen reader users (color carries zero information to a tool that never sees the rendered page), and anyone in a context where color rendering is degraded — a cheap monitor, a phone in bright sunlight washing out the color difference, grayscale mode enabled for a digital-wellbeing setting.

The fix is always redundant coding — never relying on color as the *sole* signal: pair the red border with visible text ("Email is required"), an icon that doesn't depend on color to be recognizable (an exclamation mark or X shape), and the `aria-invalid`/`aria-describedby` pairing from earlier in this topic so the same information reaches a screen reader too.

This is a WCAG requirement, not a stylistic nicety (Success Criterion 1.4.1, "Use of Color") — a design that indicates state through color alone fails a formal accessibility audit, not just an informal one.

slides.sectionTitle: Required fields and helpful hint text
slides.markdown:
Required-field indication needs the same redundant-coding treatment as errors: an asterisk alone is a color-independent visual marker, which is good, but it's meaningless to a screen reader unless the field also has the native `required` attribute (announced automatically) or an explicit `aria-required="true"`, and the asterisk's meaning itself should be spelled out once in visible text near the top of the form ("* indicates a required field") rather than assumed as universally understood convention.

Hint text — "Password must be at least 8 characters, including a number" — should use the same `aria-describedby` mechanism as error text, so a screen reader announces the requirement *before* the user submits and fails, not only after. Associating hint text this way turns a reactive error into proactive guidance, which is both a better UX for everyone and a specific, checkable accessibility improvement — a field with helpful hint text that's visually present but not wired via `aria-describedby` gives sighted users the guidance and silently withholds it from screen reader users.

A password field can simultaneously fail several rules — too short, missing a number, missing a special character — and `aria-describedby` accepts a **space-separated list of ids**, letting one field reference multiple description elements at once: ```html Must be 8+ characters with a number Missing a number ``` The screen reader announces both, in the order the ids are listed. A common mistake is overwriting the hint's id in `aria-describedby` the moment an error appears, which silently drops the general guidance right when the user needs it most (mid-correction) — the two should typically coexist, not replace each other, exactly like this multi-id pattern demonstrates.

Beyond the general keyboard and automated-tool checks from earlier topics, forms deserve a specific pass: submit the form with every field empty and confirm — with a screen reader actually running, not just by inspecting markup — that an error is announced for each field, that the announcement includes enough context to know *which* field and *why*, and that focus lands somewhere sensible (the error summary, or the first invalid field) rather than nowhere at all.

A second pass worth doing deliberately: zoom the browser to 200% and confirm error text still associates visually with its field rather than reflowing somewhere disconnected, since layout bugs at high zoom are a separate, common way error association breaks even when the underlying ARIA wiring is correct.

A complete answer to "make this form's errors accessible" covers labeling (real `<label for>` over `aria-label` wherever visible text exists), per-field error association (`aria-describedby` plus `aria-invalid`, kept in sync as validity changes), form-level dynamic feedback (an `aria-live` summary for submission-time errors, without stealing focus unnecessarily), and redundant coding (never color alone, for both errors and required-field indication).

The answer that reads as incomplete: describing only the visual error styling, or only the native HTML validation attributes, without ever mentioning how a screen reader user experiences the exact same failed submission — which is precisely the gap this topic exists to close.
